title: AI Is the Wave, the Surfer Doesn't Matter: Confessions of a Researcher at the Model Giants
dek: Pretraining hasn't hit a wall — most people who crash into one have a bug of their own. AI is fundamentally simple, because it can run experiments. The era of individual heroism is over; what matters now is organizational systematicity and being reliable.
why: The most valuable parts of this four-hour interview are the comparison of Anthropic's and Google's organizational mechanisms, the judgment on whether pretraining has hit a wall, and the counterintuitive claim that ‘AI is fundamentally simple.’ The physics section in the first half can be skipped.
who: AI practitioners, investors and founders watching how model companies organize, and how they judge the pretraining versus post-training路线; anyone who wants to understand the internal differences between Anthropic and Google DeepMind.
skip: From 1:20:59 to 1:53:47, the non-Hermitian systems, high-energy physics, and physics-to-AI portion — unless you're interested in the path of a researcher who came out of physics.

points.h: Nobody worries about catching up now, only about what to do
points.body: Yao Shunyu says that a year ago at Anthropic, what everyone worried about was how strong OpenAI's reasoning had become and whether there was any chance of catching up; now, among Gemini, OpenAI and Anthropic, none of the three would genuinely worry about failing to catch up. The harder thing has become figuring out what to do — that's a bet, and it badly needs human insight. This is a different matter from ‘model capabilities being flattened’: in terms of what users actually experience, the three still differ, but on paper (benchmark) they're all already around 80%, and being a bit higher or lower is mainly noise rather than signal.

points.h: Most people who hit the pretraining wall have a bug of their own
points.body: Many people were already discussing a few months ago whether the pretraining scaling law had run its course; Yao Shunyu's experience is that it hasn't, and he sees no sign of it ending in the next four months either. He offers three possible reasons for ‘thinking it's over’: one, believing the law's range of applicability has ended; two, believing some condition (say, data hitting a wall) can't be met; and three — which in his observation is where the vast majority fall — there's a bug in your own work that you haven't found. The bug could be a scientific hypothesis done wrong (say, token horizon, or how much data to pair with each model size wasn't chosen clearly), or it could be a pure code bug. He stresses that the progress from fixing one bug is often far greater than that from some very magical trick.

points.h: Coding exploded because the reward signal is easy to define
points.body: Coding has been developing at high speed ever since the Claude 3.5 (what outsiders call 3.6) generation, and Yao Shunyu gives two model-level reasons: first, the reward signal is very easy to define — write a feature, certain inputs produce certain outputs, and a test tells you whether it's right; second, the data has a natural foundation — GitHub aggregates decades of code from excellent programmers, and from that code you can build a great many environments. There's a third, product-level reason: good programmers write code in fairly similar styles — concise, clean, with reasonable abstractions — which makes Coding products far simpler than social or gaming products, where everyone's taste differs and you have to rely on recommendation algorithms.

points.h: Hard distillation means you don't know what you want to do; smart distillation is real multi-agent
points.body: Dario named three companies that distill him. Yao Shunyu distinguishes two kinds: hard distillation is taking a pile of generated tokens out of Claude and force-training on them — commercially unethical and intellectually stupid, because the companies doing it fundamentally don't know what they want to do, and the only thing they can do is copy others to make their numbers look good. But distillation also raises interesting scientific questions: if in your own data-generation chain you use other models as assistants, or use your own model to generate answers and other models as evaluators, that's a gray area but technically very interesting — different companies' models have very different language distributions, and merging them into one training system is真正的 multi-agent; Chinese labs may for this reason have become pioneers in multi-agent training.

points.h: Robots haven't reached their GPT-1 moment yet
points.body: Yao Shunyu searched Amazon for the prices of Chinese robots and was surprised at how cheap they were, which he sees as showing China's advantage in the hardware supply chain. But on software he hasn't quite figured it out: robot models are currently at the stage of ‘optimizing for a given environment, a given scenario’ — doing RL and building virtual environments can improve them, but there's no strong generalization. He treats the presence or absence of generalization as the watershed for many AI directions — more than a decade ago you could already train very strong models to do translation or semantic analysis, but you couldn't raise all capabilities horizontally; language crossed into that stage after Transformer and GPT, and robots haven't yet. He recommends everyone go look at robotics labs — far more interesting than language model labs.

points.h: Anthropic can go top-down, OpenAI can't
points.body: Yao Shunyu thinks it's a very unique thing that Anthropic can run a fairly top-down mechanism. The difficulty is this: the person making technical decisions must also be a decision-maker for the company — technically they have to command respect, so researchers will trust them; and at the same time they have to be a company decision-maker, so they can take responsibility for the company. Anthropic has that condition: technical leaders like Jared Kaplan and Sam are company cofounders, they make the decisions themselves, and it's their company. Other model companies find it hard: OpenAI just can't do it, and Gemini finds it relatively hard too. He adds that big companies and startups play by different rules anyway — what matters for a startup is making a bet, you have to gamble on one thing, and top-down gives it an organizational advantage over OpenAI.

points.h: AI is fundamentally simple, because it can run experiments
points.body: Yao Shunyu says this isn't a conclusion, it's a statement of his, and it can be right or wrong. He explains: the point where AI is fundamentally simple is that it can run experiments. The difference from physics is that in physics, without experimental data at that energy scale, you simply cannot understand the theory at that scale; but AI isn't bound by that — it's fine if you don't understand, it can still move forward. He can in fact now run any experiment he can think of; it just takes time to raise the compute and get the infrastructure ready, and there's no essential difficulty. So AI doesn't give people the feeling of hitting a wall: there are lots of things you can try, and it's not that your head is empty with nothing to try — it's that there are too many ideas and you have to try them one by one.

points.h: Pretraining is also a kind of RL; the difference is in the data distribution
points.body: Yao Shunyu says it's hard to state from a purely technical angle what the essential difference is between pretraining, supervised learning and RL, because pretraining and SFT are essentially no different either — it's just treating the data you get as ground truth, as expert output, and moving toward that distribution. Reinforcement learning is broader: what it outputs isn't a given expert, it's self-generated, and among the outputs there are good results and bad results — move toward the good ones, pull away from the bad ones. So pretraining and SFT are a subset of reinforcement learning. But in this era the two really are different, and the biggest difference is in the data: pretraining data needs a good enough distribution, a broad enough spread, and quality doesn't need to be very high; post-training is the reverse — the distribution is far narrower, but the data you do have has to be of very high quality.

quotes.text: I think the AI direction is fundamentally simple — there's no — I think there's no, except maybe that jump, that idea might require some very deep insight; in the process after that, a lot of the ideas are actually very trivial! Just very stupid — anyone can think of them, anyone can do them, it's just that you predicted it well and ran into the opportunity to do it.

But I think in the next six to twelve — what it currently still can't do is whether it can, from start to finish, complete a piece of AI research. For example, not only can it write the code, it can also run the experiment, and running the experiment it can see the result, and seeing the result it can analyze the result, and analyzing the result guides it on what it did wrong, and then it proposes a new hypothesis, designs new code, runs a new experiment — this chain isn't complete yet, but I think this chain is probably the thing that will gradually become complete next.

I think everyone right now is a surfer — essentially it's a wave, not you, the surfer. Is the wave AI? Yes — the thing of AI itself is this wave, it will move forward; whether or not you surf this wave, the wave will break on the shore. It's just that some people may surf this wave, and some may be a bit late and miss the crest.

I think if a researcher can't consider the whole picture, then he isn't a qualified researcher — in this era. This is, I think, a very different thing from doing research in academia, because doing research in academia is essentially a state of one person fed and the whole family not worried — I'm responsible for my project, right? I'm responsible for my reproducibility. But in a company, more often than not, I have to be responsible for the company. Yes, these are two completely different mindsets.
